nameStory: This grass is named after Ferdinand Jacob Lindheimer, a German-born botanist who collected plants in Texas during the 1840s. Though Lindheimer worked primarily in the Southwest, this panicgrass species that bears his name has made its way across much of North America. The name 'panicgrass' refers to the plant's flower clusters, called panicles, which branch out like tiny fireworks.
description: Lindheimer's panicgrass is a perennial grass that forms small clumps with slender stems reaching 1-3 feet tall. Like other rosette grasses, it produces two different types of flower clusters during the growing season - open, airy ones in late spring and smaller, hidden ones later in summer. The narrow leaves emerge from the base in a rosette pattern, giving the plant a fountain-like appearance. This grass has a delicate, wispy look that sways gracefully in the breeze.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, smooth leaves that feel almost hairless when you run your fingers along them, with tiny crooked hairs visible along the leaf edges when viewed closely

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small clumps with stems 1-3 feet tall, growing in a fountain-like rosette pattern from the base

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces two types of flower clusters - open, branched panicles in late spring that look like tiny fireworks, and smaller hidden clusters later in the season

idTips.label: Leaf Sheaths
idTips.description: The leaf sheaths (the part that wraps around the stem) are nearly smooth to the touch, lacking the dense fuzziness of some related grasses

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Look for it in areas that get wet seasonally - sandy soils near streams, lake edges, or low spots that flood briefly in spring

habitat: In New England, this grass prefers sandy soils that experience seasonal flooding or temporary wetness. You'll most likely find it along streambanks, lake shores, wet meadows, or low-lying areas in prairies and fields that collect spring runoff. It thrives in spots that are wet in spring but may dry out somewhat by late summer.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fresh green rosettes, with the first open, branched flower clusters appearing in late spring. This is when the plant is most easily identified.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering through summer with smaller, less conspicuous flower clusters. The grass maintains its green color and fountain-like growth habit throughout the warm months.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse from May through November. The grass may begin to turn golden or tan as temperatures cool, but often remains partially green.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back to brown, dried clumps. The root system remains alive underground, ready to send up new growth when spring returns.

funFact: This grass is like a botanical time-traveler - it produces two completely different types of flowers in the same year, almost like it can't decide which strategy works best! The showy spring flowers are designed to cross-pollinate with other plants, while the hidden summer flowers pollinate themselves in secret.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other rosette grasses in the same genus, especially those with similar growth habits. The key is to feel the leaves and leaf sheaths - Lindheimer's panicgrass feels much smoother and less hairy than most of its fuzzy relatives. Also check the habitat - this species prefers wetter spots than many similar-looking grasses.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this grass is extremely rare in our region and may represent an unusual introduction or a plant at the very edge of its natural range. Most field guides focus on its more common relatives, so finding this species would be quite a botanical treasure hunt!
compareHints: Among New England's rosette grasses, Lindheimer's panicgrass stands out for its nearly hairless leaves and preference for wetter soils. Most of its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses have noticeably fuzzy or hairy leaves and prefer drier conditions. The smooth leaf texture combined with its wetland habitat makes it quite distinctive from its cousins in the Dichanthelium family.

Starved witchgrass is much more delicate and sparse than its relatives like deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass, which have wider leaves and more robust growth.
Among its many witchgrass relatives, forked witchgrass stands out for its distinctly Y-shaped branching pattern.
Among its Dichanthelium relatives, broad-leaved panic grass stands out for having the widest leaves - most other rosette grasses have much narrower, linear blades.

Among its rosette grass relatives, round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is distinguished primarily by its perfectly spherical seeds - most others like hairy rosette-panicgrass or deertongue have oval or egg-shaped seeds.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, hairy rosette-panicgrass stands out for its consistently fuzzy, velvety texture - most others like deertongue feel smooth or slightly rough.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Bosc's witchgrass tends to have broader leaves than Starved Witchgrass or Slim-leaf Witchgrass, but narrower leaves than broad-leaved panic grass.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, Slim-leaf Witchgrass stands out for having the narrowest leaves - most other Dichanthelium species have broader, more oval-shaped leaves.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, variable witchgrass tends to be more adaptable to different moisture levels than most.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Small-fruited Witchgrass is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally tiny seeds - much smaller than deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass.
Wright's Rosette Grass differs from its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses by forming more perfectly circular, compact rosettes rather than loose clumps.
Compared to its Dichanthelium relatives, slender panic grass is notably more delicate and fine-textured than broad-leaved panic grass, and lacks the dense hairiness of hairy rosette-panicgrass.
Northern witchgrass is distinguished from its Dichanthelium relatives primarily by its northern range preference and smaller overall size.

Among the many panic grass relatives in New England, velvet panicum stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety texture - most other Dichanthelium species are hairy but not nearly as plush-feeling.
Unlike the more common deertongue with its broad leaves and dense shade tolerance, false bearded panic grass has much narrower leaves and prefers wet, open areas.

Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, Heller's rosette grass stands out for its strong preference for partial shade rather than full sun, and its consistently neat rosette growth pattern.

Among the rosette grasses, Scribner's Panicgrass is distinguished by its relatively narrow rosette leaves compared to broad-leaved panic grass, and its more pointed leaf tips compared to the rounded leaves of deertongue.

Eaton's Witchgrass is distinguished from its many Dichanthelium relatives by subtle differences in leaf width, flower cluster branching patterns, and seed size - characteristics that often require expert identification.

Old-field panic grass differs from its many Dichanthelium relatives primarily by habitat preference - while species like deertongue prefer shady woodlands, old-field panic grass seeks out sunny, disturbed areas.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives, old field panic grass is distinguished by its preference for truly open, disturbed habitats rather than woodland edges.
Hemlock panic grass differs from its Dichanthelium relatives by its preference for coniferous rather than deciduous woods and its particularly delicate, narrow leaves.
